hero.prompt: A friendly flat cartoon of a big round magnifying glass held over a fingertip with a neat plaster; inside the lens are five differently shaped cells: a pink dimpled disc, a purple cell with a lobed centre, a long branching cell, a tadpole-shaped cell with a long tail, and a long striped fibre.
hero.alt: A magnifying glass over a fingertip with a plaster, showing five differently shaped cells inside the lens.

slides.title: One cut, five very different cells
slides.subtitle: Five cells helped to heal this finger. They look completely different.

blocks.text: A magnifying glass over a fingertip with a plaster, showing five differently shaped cells inside the lens.
items: healing_finger_five_cells

A friendly flat cartoon of one teenage girl in a school uniform smiling and holding up one hand with a neat plaster on her finger, standing beside a kitchen table with a wooden chopping board of sliced onions.

blocks.text: What would each of these five cells NEED to do its job?

do: Display the healing-finger image and the five unlabelled cell outlines side by side.
Do not name the cells.
Tell the puzzle in your own words, or read the lines below.
say: You have all seen a cut heal. You now know cells have organelles.
Here is the puzzle for today. These five cells all live in your body right now. Each one helped heal a cut finger. But they look completely different.
Before I tell you anything, I want you to predict: what structural features would each cell need to do its job?
if_then: If a student asks which cell is which, say: Good question. Hold on to it. We will name every cell soon.
notes.why_this_works: Going back to the healing cut makes today's question feel real. Common idea: cells look different just by chance. The prediction task makes students think about jobs instead.

slides.title: Predict: what would each cell need?
slides.subtitle: Think alone. Write quietly. No talking.

blocks.text: Sketch the structural features you think each cell might need. Explain why.
items: Use your prediction sheet or notebook.
One sketch for each of the five cells.

blocks.text: Alone. Silent. 3 minutes.

do: Give each student a prediction sheet, or tell them to use their science notebook.
Start the 3-minute timer. Students work alone and in silence.
Do not circulate. Do not prompt. Keep the full wait time.
say: Take three minutes. Work alone. Sketch the features you think each cell needs, and write why.
look_for: When the timer ends, glance from the front. Does every student have at least one sketch with a reason?
Note names of students with a blank page. Give them extra support in Observe.
if_then: If a student says they do not know, say: Make a guess. Think about the job. What would help the cell do it?
notes.why_this_works: Writing alone first makes every student commit to an idea before hearing others. It shows the teacher the real starting ideas, including the idea that shape is only decoration.
answer_key: Model prediction for a cell that carries oxygen: I think it is small and round, with lots of space inside to hold oxygen, because it must carry oxygen to the cut finger.
Model prediction for a long cell: I think it is long and thin, because it must carry a pain message from the fingertip to the brain.
Model prediction for a cell that fights bacteria: I think its shape can change, because it must reach and surround bacteria in the cut.
Any sketch with a feature AND a reason linked to a job is a good prediction. A wrong prediction is fine at this stage.

slides.title: Compare your predictions
slides.subtitle: Talk with your shoulder partner

blocks.text: Compare your sketches with your shoulder partner.
items: Where do you agree?
Where do you disagree?

do: Students turn to their shoulder partner.
Start the 2-minute timer.
Listen in. Do not correct.
say: Turn to your shoulder partner. You have 2 minutes. Compare your sketches. Where do you agree? Where do you disagree?
look_for: Both partners speak. Listen for reasons about jobs, not only shapes.
if_then: If a pair finishes early, say: Pick one cell where you disagree. Can you each give a reason?
notes.why_this_works: Talking with a partner lets students test an idea in a low-risk way before they speak to the whole class.

slides.title: BEFORE — Our Predictions
slides.subtitle: Nothing is right or wrong yet. We will come back to every one.

do: Draw this table on the board under the heading BEFORE — Our Predictions.
Cold-call 5 different students, one for each cell outline.
Write the key predictions on the board in the students' own words.
Also keep the sticky-note cluster on the Driving Question Board (the lesson plan calls it 'What we THINK we know — Lesson 8').
say: Amina, tell me what feature you predicted for the round cell and why.
Thank you. I will write that on the board. We will come back to every one of these predictions.
look_for: Listen for function words, such as 'it needs to be flat to carry more oxygen'. These show students linking features to jobs.
Listen for shape-only guesses, such as 'it looks round'.
Write down the names of students who give functional reasoning. Use them as peer resources in the Explain phase.
Make sure you hear from 5 students, and that at least one student who left the page blank has a chance to speak if ready.
if_then: If a student gives a shape-only answer, ask: What job would that shape help with?
If a student gives a wrong idea, do not correct. Say: Thank you. Let's write it down. We will test it with evidence.
If a student is silent, say: Tell me what your partner said, and whether you agree.
notes.why_this_works: Recording predictions without correcting them keeps the ideas open to testing. It builds a gap between what students think and what the evidence will show.

slides.title: Observe: record what you see
slides.subtitle: Your job is NOT to explain yet

items: eyes :: Write every feature you can see.
magnifier :: Write what is missing too. Absences count!
question :: Write 'why' questions in the last column.

do: Students work in groups of four. Give each group the evidence pack: five annotated cell diagrams, two micrograph cards and one data card.
The next slides show the same five diagrams, so the lesson does not depend on printed cards.
Display the enlarged cell diagrams around the walls. Groups may walk and look at any time.
If students handle printed micrograph cards, they wash their hands before and after.
say: Your job right now is NOT to explain. Your job is to observe carefully and record what you see.
For every feature you notice, write it down. For features that are absent, like a nucleus that is not there, write that down too. Absences are just as important as presences.
if_then: If a group asks 'why', say: Write that question in the Questions Raised column. That is exactly what the Explain phase is for.
notes.why_this_works: Splitting what you see from why it is so stops students from jumping to explanations. Recording absences trains a higher-level skill: using what is missing as evidence.

slides.title: Your observation table
slides.subtitle: Copy this table into your own book

do: Each student copies the observation table into their own book.
Groups fill in one row for each cell as the next slides show it.
Circulate. Check the table is set up correctly.
say: Copy this table. You will fill in one row for each cell. Work as a group, but everyone writes in their own book.
look_for: Check that every student has the table with four column headings in their book.
if_then: If a student has copied only some columns, say: You need all four columns. The last one is for your questions.
notes.why_this_works: One fixed table for all five cells makes recording the same each time. This sets up the pattern search in Explain.
answer_key: Red blood cell: observed - biconcave disc, cell membrane, cytoplasm packed with haemoglobin; absent - no nucleus; question - Why no nucleus? Why this shape?
White blood cell: observed - irregular shape, lobed nucleus, many lysosomes, flexible membrane; absent - no fixed regular shape; question - Why so many lysosomes?
Nerve cell: observed - long axon, myelin sheath, dendrites, synaptic knobs (axon terminals), nucleus; absent - no tail, no stripes; question - Why is the axon so long?
Sperm cell: observed - streamlined head, mid-piece packed with mitochondria, long flagellum; absent - no dendrites, no long axon; question - Why so many mitochondria in the mid-piece?
Muscle cell: observed - many mitochondria, parallel myofilaments, several nuclei; absent - not just one nucleus; question - Why so many mitochondria?
Accept any honest observation that can be seen in the diagram.

slides.title: Red blood cell
slides.subtitle: Observe and record. Do not explain yet.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.
Pack notes: biconcave disc · no nucleus · packed with haemoglobin

do: Show the red blood cell drawing while groups fill in the first row of the table.
Circulate. Narrate what you see without explaining, for example: I can see your group has noticed the biconcave shape. Keep going. What else?
say: Record what you can see. Also record what is missing. A missing nucleus is evidence too.
look_for: At 3 tables: features are specific, such as 'no nucleus', not vague, such as 'looks different'.
if_then: If a group asks why, say: Write that question in the Questions Raised column. We will answer it soon.
If a group writes 'looks different', say: Different how? Name one feature you can point to.
notes.why_this_works: Naming features without explaining them keeps students in the evidence-gathering mindset. Common wrong idea: shape is only how a cell looks. We hold that for the Explain phase.
answer_key: Red blood cell: observed - biconcave disc (dip on both faces), cell membrane, cytoplasm packed with haemoglobin; absent - no nucleus; question - Why is there no nucleus? Why this shape?
notes.science_note: In humans, mature red blood cells have lost their nucleus.

slides.title: White blood cell (neutrophil)
slides.subtitle: Observe and record. Do not explain yet.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.
Pack notes: irregular lobed nucleus · many lysosomes · flexible membrane

do: Show the white blood cell drawing while groups fill in the second row of the table.
The drawing does not label lysosomes. Read the pack notes aloud so every group has them.
Circulate and narrate what you see. Do not explain.
say: What do you notice about the shape? What about the nucleus? Write it down.
look_for: At 3 tables: the lobed nucleus and the irregular shape are recorded.
if_then: If a group asks what lysosomes do, say: Good question. Write it in Questions Raised. We will find out in Explain.
notes.why_this_works: Students gather the same kind of evidence for each cell before they look for a pattern across all five.
answer_key: White blood cell (neutrophil): observed - irregular shape, lobed nucleus, many lysosomes, flexible membrane; absent - no fixed regular shape; question - Why so many lysosomes? Why a lobed nucleus?

slides.title: Nerve cell (neuron)
slides.subtitle: Observe and record. Do not explain yet.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.
Pack notes: long axon · myelin sheath · dendrites · synaptic knobs

do: Show the nerve cell drawing while groups fill in the third row.
This is about the middle of the Observe phase. Do the mid-observation check: cold-call one group.
The drawing label 'axon terminals' is the same as 'synaptic knobs' in the pack notes.
say: Group 3, read me one feature you noticed about the nerve cell that surprised you.
look_for: Look at 4 tables: the red blood cell and white blood cell rows have entries in all four columns.
In the cold-call answer, listen for a specific feature, such as 'long axon', not 'it looks different'.
if_then: If the group names no feature, say: Look at the drawing again. Point to the longest part. What is it called?
If a table has an empty Questions Raised column, say: If you were that red blood cell squeezed through a very narrow tube, what question would YOU have?
notes.why_this_works: A check in the middle of data collection lets the teacher fix vague recording while there is still time to improve it.
answer_key: Nerve cell: observed - long axon, myelin sheath, dendrites, synaptic knobs (axon terminals), nucleus; absent - no tail, no stripes; question - Why is the axon so long?

slides.title: Sperm cell
slides.subtitle: Observe and record. Do not explain yet.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.
Pack notes: streamlined head · mid-piece packed with mitochondria · long flagellum

do: Show the sperm cell drawing while groups fill in the fourth row.
Use calm, matter-of-fact language. Keep the focus on structure.
Circulate and narrate what you see.
say: Where are the mitochondria in this cell? Write down where you find them.
look_for: At 3 tables: the mid-piece and the flagellum are both recorded.
if_then: If students giggle, say: This is a cell like any other. Look at its parts and write what you see.
notes.why_this_works: Using the same recording routine for every cell keeps the focus on structure and builds the pattern students will use in Explain.
answer_key: Sperm cell: observed - streamlined head, mid-piece packed with mitochondria, long flagellum (tail); absent - no dendrites, no long axon; question - Why so many mitochondria in the mid-piece?

slides.title: Muscle cell
slides.subtitle: Observe and record. Do not explain yet.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.
Pack notes: many mitochondria · parallel myofilaments · several nuclei

do: Show the muscle cell drawing while groups fill in the last row.
The drawing says 'myofibrils'. The pack notes say 'myofilaments'. Tell students to use the word in their pack.
Circulate and narrate what you see.
say: Count the nuclei if you can. Count how many mitochondria you can see. Write it down.
look_for: At 3 tables: 'many mitochondria' and 'more than one nucleus' are recorded.
if_then: If students say the muscle cell is the same as a nerve cell because both are long, say: Look at the parts inside. What is different?
notes.why_this_works: By the fifth cell, students begin to compare cells without being told to. This sets up the pattern search in Explain.
answer_key: Muscle cell: observed - many mitochondria, parallel myofilaments, several nuclei; absent - not just one nucleus; question - Why so many mitochondria?

slides.title: Micrograph cards and data card
slides.subtitle: Look at the evidence. Record what you see.

blocks.text: Look at your two micrograph cards: normal and sickle red blood cells; a nerve cell stained with methylene blue.
Data card: A red blood cell lives for about 120 days and makes about 170,000 circuits of the body. A neutrophil lives for about 6 hours during active infection.

do: Groups look at the two printed micrograph cards. If the cards are missing, project them from the teacher pack.
Students add what they see on the cards to their table.
Read the data card aloud once. Students write one question about it in Questions Raised.
At the end, say pens down. Do not discuss the sickle cells yet. That is for Explain.
say: Pens down. Every group should have at least 3 structural features recorded for each cell.
Do not tell me why yet. Keep your questions. We will use them in the next phase.
look_for: Check 5 observation tables: at least 3 specific features per cell, and entries in all four columns for at least 4 of the 5 cells.
Listen for groups linking the 120-day life of a red blood cell to having no nucleus. Note them for cold-calls in Explain.
if_then: If a group has an empty Questions Raised column, say: If you were a red blood cell squeezed through a capillary thinner than you, what question would YOU have?
If a group writes only 'sickle cells look different', say: Different how? Describe the shape of each one.
If a group has fewer than 3 features for a cell, say: Look at the diagram again. Which parts can you name?
notes.why_this_works: A final check of the tables tells the teacher whether students have good evidence to explain from. A group with weak evidence will only guess in Explain.
answer_key: Card 1: normal red blood cells are round discs with a dip in the middle; sickle cells are long and curved, like a crescent.
Card 2: the nerve cell is a long thin cell with branches; the methylene blue makes it easy to see.
Data card question, for example: Why does a neutrophil live for hours but a red blood cell for months?

slides.title: Now we explain
slides.subtitle: From 'what do I see?' to 'why is it like that?'

blocks.text: What job does each feature help the cell do?

items: question :: WHY does each feature exist?
puzzle :: What job does it help the cell do?
bandage :: How does it link to the cut finger?

do: Tell students you are moving from observing to explaining.
Point to the three questions. They are the questions for every cell.
say: Now we move from observing to explaining. For every feature you recorded, answer three things. Why does that feature exist? What job does it help the cell do? And how does that connect to the day a student in Nairobi cut their finger?
if_then: If students ask whether they can use the textbook, say: Use your own table first. Your evidence is the starting point.
notes.why_this_works: Three short questions give students a repeatable chain of reasoning to use for each cell. Common wrong idea: shape is decoration. These questions ask students to link shape to a job.

slides.title: Structure–function organiser
slides.subtitle: Work in your group. Link each feature to its job.

do: Groups of four keep the same groups as in Observe.
Hand out the Structure-Function Graphic Organiser, or students copy the table.
Start the 16-minute timer.
Circulate and use the targeted prompts below.
Prompt for the red blood cell: You said no nucleus. What does a nucleus do? So what happens to all that space inside the cell?
Prompt for the nerve cell: You said long axon. How far does a pain signal travel from a fingertip to the brain? What does length make possible?
Prompt for the muscle cell: You said many mitochondria. What do mitochondria produce? Why would a muscle cell need a lot of that?
say: For every feature you recorded, write why that feature exists. What job does it help the cell do? And how does it connect to the cut finger?
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after each prompt when you ask a group
look_for: Check 4 groups: each has a clear explanation (feature, then job) for at least 3 cells, and the 'Link to the healing cut' column is filled.
Listen for words like 'because', 'so', 'which means'. These show causal reasoning. A lower answer only describes: 'the red blood cell has no nucleus and carries oxygen'.
Note groups that link a feature to a function without help. Use them in the share-out.
if_then: If a group only describes a feature, say: You told me what it has. Now tell me what that lets the cell do.
If a group is stuck on a link to the healing cut, say: What does the finger need at the cut? Oxygen? Fighting bacteria? A pain message? Movement?
If a group writes 'it is just built that way', say: Cells are not built randomly. What job could this feature help with?
notes.why_this_works: Group talk with targeted questions pushes students from describing to explaining. The link column keeps the shape-and-job idea tied to the healing cut.
answer_key: Red blood cell: biconcave disc, no nucleus; no nucleus leaves more space for haemoglobin, so the cell carries more oxygen; it delivers oxygen to the healing tissue.
White blood cell: irregular flexible shape, many lysosomes; a flexible shape lets it reach and surround bacteria, and lysosomes digest them; it engulfs bacteria at the wound.
Nerve cell: long axon with a myelin sheath; the long axon lets a signal travel a long way, for example fingertip to brain; it carries the pain signal from the cut.

Sperm cell: flagellum, mid-piece packed with mitochondria; the flagellum lets it swim and the mitochondria release the energy for swimming; it is not directly involved in healing, but it shows that a very special shape fits one job.
Muscle cell: many mitochondria, parallel myofilaments; mitochondria release energy and myofilaments allow the cell to contract; movement keeps the wounded finger protected.
The red blood cell row also gets sickle-cell evidence after the sickle-cell slides.
notes.science_note: A mature red blood cell has no nucleus, so it has more room for haemoglobin.

slides.title: Share out: Claim, Evidence, Reasoning
slides.subtitle: One cell at a time. Listen, then add or challenge.

items: Claim :: What is this cell built to do?
Evidence :: What did you observe?
Reasoning :: Why does that feature help the job?

do: Project a completed organiser. Click through one cell at a time.
Cold-call one group per cell. Choose groups you noted as strong in Observe for harder cells, and a quieter group for the first one.
After each answer, ask the whole class if any group wants to add or challenge.
For the nerve cell, you may use the neuron video or reading from ARES after the group has answered. Preview first.
say: Group 2, give me your CER for the red blood cell. Claim, Evidence, Reasoning.
Does any group want to add or challenge?
look_for: Listen for causal language: because, therefore, which means, as a result.
Target answer: 'The red blood cell has no nucleus because that leaves more room for haemoglobin, which means it can carry more oxygen to the healing tissue.'
Note which groups give only description, so you can follow up with them.
if_then: If a group gives only description, say: That is the evidence. What is your reasoning? Why does it help?
If a group gives a wrong reason, say: Thank you. Who can add to that or challenge it using the evidence?
notes.why_this_works: Claim, Evidence, Reasoning turns a list of features into an explanation. Hearing other groups add or challenge lets students test their own reasoning against evidence.
answer_key: Red blood cell: Claim - it is built to carry oxygen. Evidence - biconcave disc, no nucleus, packed with haemoglobin. Reasoning - no nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin, so it carries more oxygen to the healing tissue.
White blood cell: Claim - it is built to destroy bacteria. Evidence - flexible shape and many lysosomes. Reasoning - the flexible shape lets it surround bacteria and the lysosomes digest them.

Nerve cell: Claim - it is built to carry signals far. Evidence - a long axon with a myelin sheath. Reasoning - length lets one cell reach from the fingertip towards the brain, and the sheath helps the signal move quickly.
Sperm cell: Claim - it is built to swim. Evidence - a flagellum and a mid-piece packed with mitochondria. Reasoning - the flagellum moves the cell and the mitochondria release the energy for it.
Muscle cell: Claim - it is built to contract. Evidence - many mitochondria and parallel myofilaments. Reasoning - mitochondria release energy for contraction and myofilaments make the cell shorten.

slides.title: A puzzle: sickle-cell red blood cells
slides.subtitle: Look at the shapes. Use your micrograph card too.

blocks.text: A drawing of normal red cells, round with a dip in the middle, beside sickle-shaped red cells, long and curved like a crescent.
items: sickle_vs_normal_red_cells

A friendly flat cartoon of two groups of red cells side by side on a pale background: on the left several round red discs with a dip in the middle, on the right several long curved crescent-shaped dark red cells.

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.

do: Display the sickle-cell comparison. Students can also hold up the micrograph card from Observe.
Be sensitive. Sickle-cell disease is a medical condition. Use respectful language only.
If a student shares a personal or family experience, thank them with care and bring the focus back to the science.
say: Look at the shape of the normal cells and the shape of the sickle cells. What is different?
look_for: Listen for students describing the shapes: round discs with a dip, and long curved cells.
if_then: If a student says 'the cell is sick', say: Describe its shape. What do you see?
notes.why_this_works: Looking first at the shape, before the question, keeps students describing evidence. The sickle cell gives a real case where a change in shape changes the job.

slides.title: Argue from the evidence
slides.subtitle: Talk with your partner. Use what you can see.

blocks.text: Sickle cells still contain haemoglobin. So why do people with sickle-cell disease get anaemia and blocked vessels?

do: Ask the question and wait 10 seconds in silence.
Pairs argue from the evidence for 3 minutes.
Listen in. Do not give the answer.
say: Here is the argument question. The sickle cell still contains haemoglobin. So why does the shape matter?
Talk with your partner. Use what you can see in the picture.
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds of silence after the question, then 3 minutes of pair talk
look_for: Listen to 4 pairs: do they mention shape, small blood vessels, or oxygen?
if_then: If a pair says 'the cell is sick', say: Look at its shape. What does the shape do when the cell must travel through a very small tube?
If a pair is silent, say: Think about a round, smooth cell and a long, curved cell moving through the same narrow space.
notes.why_this_works: The sickle cell makes the idea 'shape is function' something students can test, not just accept. Common wrong idea: shape does not matter if the cell has the right contents.

slides.title: Write your CER: shape and function
slides.subtitle: Use the sickle-cell evidence

items: Claim :: The problem is...
Evidence :: In the picture I can see...
Reasoning :: This matters because...

blocks.text: Write 2 or 3 sentences. Use the word 'because'.
items: Add your answer to the red blood cell row of your organiser.

do: Cold-call 3 students to give their CER aloud. Choose one who showed functional reasoning in Predict, one who was unsure, and one who has not spoken yet.
Then all students write their own CER in the red blood cell row of the organiser.
Count how many of the 3 cold-called students give a complete shape, blockage and function link.
say: Make a claim about what the problem is. Give evidence from the picture. Give reasoning that connects shape to function.
This is your strongest evidence yet that shape is function. Shape is not decoration.
look_for: Listen for the link: the abnormal shape stops the cell passing through small vessels and reduces how well it carries oxygen.
Check 5 organiser rows: each has a claim, evidence from the picture, and a reason using 'because'.
This is the key check of the lesson. At least 2 of the 3 cold-called students (60%) should give the full shape, blockage and function link.
if_then: If fewer than 2 of 3 can give the full link, pause and use the blood vessel idea: Think of a narrow gate. A round smooth cell passes through easily. A long curved cell gets stuck. What happens to the oxygen it carries?
If a student only says 'it is a different shape', say: And what does that shape stop the cell doing?
If a student says 'it has no haemoglobin', say: Look at the question again. The cell has haemoglobin. So what else is the problem?
notes.why_this_works: Writing a CER after the oral argument asks every student to build the explanation themselves. Common wrong idea: shape does not matter if the cell has the right contents. This task tests that idea.
answer_key: Claim: The sickle shape stops the red blood cell doing its job. Evidence: In the micrograph, normal cells are round discs but sickle cells are long and curved. Reasoning: A curved cell cannot pass through small blood vessels easily, so it can block them, and it carries oxygen less well, so the person has anaemia. This shows that shape determines function.

slides.title: Driving Question Board: your note
slides.subtitle: Evidence from today, and one new question

blocks.text: Why do cells in our body look so different from each other, and how does the shape of a cell determine the job it can do?
Front: what I now understand. Use something we saw today. Back: one new question.

do: Give each student a sticky note or index card.
Start the 3-minute timer. Work is individual and silent.
Students post their notes on the Driving Question Board in two columns: 'What we NOW understand' and 'New questions we have'.
Scan the board. Pick 4 or 5 notes to read in the next slide.
say: Three minutes. Alone and silent. Write one thing you now understand about our driving question that you did not understand at the start of today's lesson. Use something we saw today, not the textbook.
On the back, write one question this lesson has raised for you.
look_for: Check all notes after posting: every student has both an update and a new question.
The update uses something seen today, such as the micrograph, a diagram or the data card.

After the lesson, sort the notes into three piles: target understanding with structure and function language, partial understanding with structure but no function, and a misconception or surface answer.
if_then: If a student writes only 'cells look different', say: Say why they look different. Use one cell we saw today.
If a student writes a fact from a book, say: Choose something we saw or measured today. What did the evidence show?
If a student cannot think of a question, say: What would you still like to know about how cells know what to do?
notes.why_this_works: Writing both an update and a question makes students check what they know and where their knowledge stops. The board makes the class's learning visible.
answer_key: Front: Cells look different because they do different jobs. A red blood cell has no nucleus so it has more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen to the cut. Back: Does every organ have its own special cells?

slides.title: Reading the board together
slides.subtitle: What do we understand now? What is still puzzling?

blocks.text: Claim: cells look different BECAUSE they do different jobs. Does today's evidence support it?
Cell specialisation: a cell has a special shape and parts that fit its job.

do: Read 4 or 5 notes aloud. Choose a mix of strong explanations and interesting new questions.
Ask which new questions the next lesson might answer, and which may take us to the end of the unit.
Point to the healing-cut image. Show how today moved the class from 'cells look different' to 'cells look different because they do different jobs'.
Take a quick class vote on the claim. Ask for thumbs up or thumbs down. Count and write the number on the board.
Click to show the name only AFTER the vote and discussion.
Write the 3 or 4 best new questions on the permanent Driving Question Board display. Track them over the next lessons.
say: At the start of this unit, we asked: how does the body send exactly the right response to heal that cut?
Today you built part of that answer. The right response is possible because each cell has a shape that is right for its job. That is cell specialisation.
Which of these questions do you think we will answer next lesson? Which might take us to the end of the unit?
look_for: Count the thumbs in the vote. Most students should say yes and give an example from today's evidence.
Ask 2 students to name the evidence that supports their vote. Listen for a cell, a feature and a job.
Listen to see if any new questions are about organs, tissues or systems. These show readiness for later lessons.
if_then: If a student asks how cells know what to become, say: Great question. That is a big one for later. We will park it on the board as a question for future learning.
If students vote no, say: Tell us which evidence does not fit. Let's test it.
If only a few students can give evidence, say: Look at your organiser. Find one cell, one feature and one job.
notes.why_this_works: Reading the board aloud and voting on a claim lets students see how evidence builds an idea. Naming 'cell specialisation' after the understanding makes the word mean something.

slides.title: Revise your cumulative model
slides.subtitle: Lesson 8: a new layer called Cell Specialisation

items: palette :: Use a NEW colour for today.
microscope :: Add at least two specialised animal cells.
clipboard :: For each cell: 3 features and what each one does.
arrow_right :: Draw an arrow linking each cell to the healing cut.
memo :: Add a new layer called 'Cell Specialisation'.

do: Students take out their cumulative cell model.
Read the five revisions aloud, one at a time.
Tell students to use a new colour so their changes show clearly.
say: Take out your cumulative model. It is Lesson 8 of 12. Your model should already show organelles and the differences between plant and animal cells.
Today we add a new layer: specialisation. Add at least two specialised cells with full notes. Connect each one with an arrow back to the healing cut.
if_then: If a student has lost their model, say: Start on a fresh page. Add today's layer and your earlier work as you remember it.
notes.why_this_works: Adding to the same model, in a new colour, shows how thinking grows over the unit. Students see that today's idea is one more layer, not a new topic.

slides.title: Add specialised cells to your model
slides.subtitle: Cell → feature → job → healing cut

blocks.text: Example: RED BLOOD CELL → delivers oxygen to healing tissue → biconcave shape + no nucleus = maximum haemoglobin capacity.
items: Write: This model is based on evidence from ...
Model claim: In our body, cell shape is not random. It is determined by function.

do: Start the 9-minute timer.
Circulate. Narrate what you see, for example: I can see Baraka has drawn the nerve cell with a long axon. Baraka, add a label explaining WHY the axon is long and connect it to the cut finger.
At the 7-minute mark, say two minutes remain. Check that students have written the model claim at the bottom.
Stamp or initial completed models.
Collect 5 or 6 models at the end (change the students each lesson). Write feedback before the next lesson. Pick 2 or 3 to show next lesson.
say: Add at least two specialised cells with full notes. For each cell, give three features and the job each feature does. Draw an arrow back to the healing cut.
Write where your evidence comes from: This model is based on evidence from, and name something you saw today.
Two minutes left. Make sure you have written the model claim at the bottom.
look_for: Check 8 models: each has at least two new specialised cells, with three features, the job of each, and an arrow to the healing cut.
The arrow to the healing cut is the highest level of connection. Students who only describe a shape, such as 'biconcave', need follow-up next lesson.
Check that students cite evidence, for example 'from the organiser' or 'from the sickle-cell micrograph'.
if_then: If a student only labels shapes, say: Add what each feature lets the cell do. Then draw the arrow to the finger.
If a student is stuck, say: Choose the cell you understand best. What is its job in healing the cut?
If a student has no evidence line, say: Which picture, card or table showed you this?
notes.why_this_works: The model joins three ideas in one drawing: structure, function and the healing cut. Asking for evidence keeps the model based on what students saw, not only on what they were told.
answer_key: Model for the nerve cell: NERVE CELL → carries the pain signal from the fingertip to the brain → long axon = the signal travels a long way; myelin sheath = the signal travels faster; dendrites = receive the signal. This model is based on evidence from the organiser and the nerve cell drawing.

Model for the muscle cell: MUSCLE CELL → moves the finger away and keeps the wound protected → many mitochondria = release energy; parallel myofilaments = make the cell shorten; several nuclei. This model is based on evidence from the organiser and the muscle cell drawing.
Model claim written at the bottom: In our body, cell shape is not random. It is determined by function.

slides.title: Test our model claim
slides.subtitle: Does it work for all five cells?

blocks.text: Does our claim hold for ALL five cells? Thumbs up, sideways or down.
Write one sentence about the next lesson.
items: Next lesson I predict ... because ...

do: Cold-call one student to read their model claim aloud.
Ask the class the question and count the thumbs.
Talk to any students with sideways thumbs before you close.
Students write one sentence predicting what the next lesson might be about, with a reason.
say: Does this claim hold for all five cells we studied today? Thumbs up if yes. Thumbs sideways if you are not sure.
Your model is getting more powerful. We keep adding to it, lesson by lesson, as we get closer to explaining the healing cut.
Now write one sentence: next lesson I predict, because.
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after the question before asking for thumbs
look_for: Count the thumbs. Most students should have thumbs up.
Check 5 prediction sentences: each has a reason.
For sideways thumbs, ask the student which cell they are unsure about.
if_then: If students are unsure about the sperm cell, say: Look at the feature and the job. Does the shape fit the job? What does the cell NOT do in healing?
If a student cannot predict, say: What is still puzzling on the Driving Question Board? Write about that.
notes.why_this_works: Testing the claim against all five cells shows students that a good idea in science works across the evidence. A prediction for next time keeps the story going.
answer_key: Yes, the claim holds. Red blood cell: shape and no nucleus carry oxygen. White blood cell: flexible shape and lysosomes deal with bacteria. Nerve cell: long axon carries signals. Sperm cell: flagellum and mitochondria help it swim. Muscle cell: mitochondria and myofilaments allow movement.
Prediction example: Next lesson I predict we will learn about more specialised cells, because other living things also need cells that do special jobs.

lesson_oneliner: Five cells helped heal one cut. Why do they look so different?
purpose: Students discover that cells in the body look different because they do different jobs. Shape and parts fit the job.
They study five specialised animal cells: red blood, white blood, nerve, sperm and muscle cells.
They use the sickle-cell red blood cell as a real case. The cell still holds haemoglobin, but its changed shape changes its function.
This lesson is the pivot of the evidence-gathering lessons. It answers the unit puzzle: why do cells that came from the same organism look so different?
Common wrong idea: cell shape is only decoration. Predict, Observe and the sickle-cell argument all test this idea.
before_class: Print one evidence pack per group of four: five annotated cell diagrams, two micrograph cards (normal vs sickle red blood cells; a nerve cell stained with methylene blue) and one data card.
Prepare prediction sheets, or tell students to use their science notebooks.
Prepare copies of the Structure-Function Graphic Organiser, or students copy the table from the slide.
Post enlarged cell diagrams around the classroom walls.
Have sticky notes or index cards ready for every student.
Set up the Driving Question Board with two columns: 'What we NOW understand' and 'New questions we have'. Keep the 'What we THINK we know — Lesson 8' cluster.
Prepare a completed organiser to project during the share-out.
Check that students have their cumulative cell model and a pen or pencil in a new colour.
Preview any ARES resource before use. None is needed to run the lesson.
Plan how you will speak about sickle-cell disease with care. Students or families may live with it.
do_not_show: Do not show the 'Red blood cell' to 'Muscle cell' drawing slides until students have written and shared their predictions.
Do not show the 'A puzzle: sickle-cell red blood cells' slide until the Observe phase is finished. Students may look at the micrograph card in Observe, but do not discuss it until Explain.
Do not project the completed organiser or any answer until groups have finished their own organiser.
Do not show the ARES neuron video or reading until the nerve cell group has given its answer.
Do not click to show the words 'Cell specialisation' on the 'Reading the board together' slide until after the class vote and discussion.
so_far: You have learned about cell parts, compared plant and animal cells, and looked at onion and cheek cells under the microscope.
goals: Explain how a cell's structure fits its function.
Describe how five animal cells are built for their jobs.
Explain, with evidence, why cell shape matters.

key_words.definition: The shape of a cell and the parts inside it.
The job that a cell or a cell part does.
What we see or measure that helps us test an idea.
The science idea that links your evidence to your claim.

resource_notes.note: Red blood cells are a core cell in this lesson, but this video explains their structure and function. Use it after Explain, as revision or consolidation.
A nerve cell reading explains the structure-function link that students should predict first. Use after the 'Structure–function organiser' in Explain. Check it covers axon, myelin and dendrites.
Kiswahili red blood cell video gives away the explanation of shape and function. Use after Explain as support for Kiswahili speakers or as revision.
Nerve cell practice questions test understanding students are meant to build. Use after 'Share out: Claim, Evidence, Reasoning' as a check; preview the question level first.
Neuron anatomy video fits the Explain phase and supports the nerve cell row of the organiser. Preview the length, since it may go beyond Grade 10 detail.
Skeletal muscle cell video suits muscle cell structure, but DQB is a note-writing slot. Preview it; better shown during Explain or before the model task.
Kiswahili neuron video supports the nerve cell annotations in the model. Preview it, and it may fit better during Explain, before 'Add specialised cells to your model'.
Nerve cells and impulses reading helps learners annotate the neuron, but covers impulse detail beyond the lesson. Preview and select only the structure-function parts.

summary.observe_prompt: Name the five cells and one feature you saw on each.
summary.learn_prompt: What does a feature tell us about a cell's job? What happens when the shape changes?
summary.explain_prompt: How do these cells help heal the cut finger?
summary.next_lesson: Do plants have specialised cells too? Look at a bean seedling and see.
summary.answer_observe: I looked at drawings and cards of five animal cells. The red blood cell is a biconcave disc with no nucleus. The white blood cell has an irregular shape, a lobed nucleus and many lysosomes. The nerve cell has a long axon, a myelin sheath and dendrites. The sperm cell has a streamlined head, a mid-piece full of mitochondria and a long flagellum. The muscle cell has many mitochondria, parallel myofilaments and several nuclei. Normal red blood cells are round discs with a dip. Sickle cells are long and curved.
summary.answer_learn: Cell specialisation means a cell has a special shape and special parts that fit its job. The features are not random. No nucleus, a long axon and a flagellum are all adaptations to function. When the shape changes, as in sickle-cell anaemia, the cell cannot do its job well. This is evidence that shape determines function.
summary.answer_explain: Red blood cells deliver oxygen to the healing tissue. White blood cells engulf bacteria at the wound. Nerve cells carry the pain signal from the finger. Muscle cells let the finger move away and keep the wound protected. The sperm cell is not involved in healing, but it shows how a very special shape fits one job. Claim: cell shape is the physical basis of cell function. Evidence: the sickle cell has haemoglobin but its curved shape stops it passing through small vessels. Reasoning: a cell can only do its job if its shape fits the job.
reflection: Were students' first predictions only about shape, or did they link shape to a job? If mostly shape only, plan a short review of cell functions at the start of the next lesson.
Did the sickle-cell argument work? Could at least 60% of the cold-called students give the shape, blockage and function link? If not, plan another example to practise it before moving on.

What new questions appeared on the Driving Question Board? Sort them. Which need more work on single cells, and which are ready for the next level? Park questions about how cells know what to become as future learning.
On the models you collected, did students draw the arrow back to the healing cut? If not, show one strong model at the start of the next lesson and ask what makes it more powerful.
Did the timing work? If the Explain phase ran over, plan to move part of the sickle-cell discussion to the start of the next lesson rather than cutting Model Building.

Our big question is still the same: why do cells in our body look so different, and how does the shape of a cell decide its job?

Read each key word with its plain meaning.
Tell students they will use claim, evidence and reasoning later in the lesson.
Do not explain the goals in detail. Keep this to about one minute.
say: By the end of today you can explain how a cell's structure fits its function.
You can describe how five animal cells are built for their jobs. And you can use evidence to explain why cell shape matters.
These five words will help you today. Listen for them as we go.
goals_notes.why_this_works: Plain goals and a few clear words let students know what to look for. The key words are tools for thinking, so they do not give away what students will find.
